name: Trajectory
intro: Trajectory asks what AI systems will actually be able to do: which capabilities, through which mechanisms, and on what timeline — keeping claims about what is impossible in principle distinct from claims about what is merely far off. It spans the ceiling of the current paradigm, the ingredients still missing, and how far autonomy, embodiment, and self-improvement can go.

qs.q: How far can transformers, reinforcement learning, tool use, and inference-time reasoning progress without a fundamentally new architecture?
qs.n: The scaling hypothesis bet that capability comes from scale, not cleverness. The live question is whether pretraining returns are genuinely diminishing — itself disputed — and if so, whether RL on verifiable tasks and test-time compute offset them, or the paradigm tops out short of general competence.
qs.crux: Are current architectures sufficient for broadly superhuman intelligence?

links.t: Will scaling work?
The Era of Experience

qs.q: How much future progress will come from compute, algorithms, data, inference-time search, better environments, or system-level scaffolding?
qs.n: Decompositions of historical progress attribute gains roughly evenly to compute scaling and algorithmic efficiency. Which input dominates going forward determines who can compete, what governance levers exist, and how abruptly progress could slow.

links.t: The Bitter Lesson
Algorithmic Progress in Language Models

qs.q: Can synthetic data, self-play, simulation, and interaction substitute for the finite supply of high-quality human-generated data?
qs.n: Frontier pretraining has plausibly consumed most high-quality public text. Synthetic data clearly works where verification is cheap (math, code); whether it generalizes to open-ended domains without model collapse is contested.

links.t: Will We Run Out of Data?
AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data

qs.q: Will chips, fabrication, memory, networking, electricity, cooling, land, or capital materially slow progress?
qs.n: Training compute has grown ~4–5× per year. Power availability, HBM supply, advanced packaging, and the sheer capital intensity of frontier clusters are the leading candidates for what binds first.

links.t: Can AI Scaling Continue Through 2030?
Announcing GPT-4.5: “out of GPUs” — compute as the binding constraint, live

qs.q: Will systems become broadly competent across unfamiliar domains, or remain highly capable but fundamentally jagged?
qs.n: Today's models are superhuman on some tasks and fail at things a child can do — the 'jagged frontier.' Whether jaggedness is a transient artifact of training distributions or intrinsic to the paradigm is the crux.

links.t: Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence
Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier
“Jagged Intelligence” — SOTA models solve impressive problems while failing at simple ones

qs.q: Are continual learning, causal reasoning, world models, embodied experience, persistent memory, or social understanding still major unsolved problems?
qs.n: LeCun and others argue autoregressive LLMs structurally lack world models and continual learning; scaling proponents reply that these emerge with scale or can be scaffolded around. Continual learning is increasingly cited as the binding gap.

links.t: Why I don't think AGI is right around the corner
A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence
Why AGI is still a decade away: agents lack continual learning — “the decade of agents”

qs.q: Can systems reason accurately outside familiar patterns rather than merely producing convincing-looking chains of thought?
qs.n: Reasoning models raise accuracy, but performance degrades under superficial variations of familiar problems, and stated chains of thought are often not faithful accounts of the underlying computation.

links.t: GSM-Symbolic: Limitations of Mathematical Reasoning in LLMs
Reasoning models don't always say what they think

qs.q: Can AI learn new domains from small amounts of experience as effectively as capable humans?
qs.n: Humans learn new skills from orders of magnitude less data. Chollet argues sample-efficient skill acquisition is what intelligence is — making learning efficiency a definition, not just a milestone.

links.t: On the Measure of Intelligence
Building Machines That Learn and Think Like People

qs.q: What should count as human-level or general intelligence, and would we recognize it before its consequences became obvious?
qs.n: Definitions have drifted from Turing tests to economic thresholds to capability profiles. Without agreed criteria, arrival may be declared only in retrospect — after the consequences have already begun compounding.

links.t: Levels of AGI
A Definition of AGI
o3 scores 87.5% on ARC-AGI — a step-change in novel-task adaptation, and still not AGI

qs.q: When, if ever, might broadly human-level systems arrive?
qs.n: Expert forecasts span decades and have shortened with each survey wave. Most trajectory disagreements are actually about timing, not possibility — yet 'that cannot work' and 'that will not work soon' are routinely argued as if they were the same claim.

links.t: Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI
Literature Review of Transformative AI Timelines
AI Timelines: Where the Arguments, and the “Experts,” Stand

qs.q: How quickly will the length of tasks agents can complete reliably grow — from minutes to days, months, or entire organizational projects?
qs.n: METR's 2025 measurement found the length of software tasks agents complete at 50% reliability doubling roughly every seven months, with faster doubling among recent models. Extrapolating that curve is a key input to short-timeline forecasts.
qs.crux: How rapidly will reliable autonomous task horizons grow?

links.t: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks
Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks (paper)

qs.q: Can agents maintain coherent memories, plans, goals, and identities across long periods and changing circumstances?
qs.n: Long-running agents drift: extended-operation benchmarks and real deployments show degrading coherence, hallucinated context, and occasional identity breakdown well before task-horizon limits are reached.

links.t: Vending-Bench: Long-Term Coherence of Autonomous Agents

qs.q: Can agents recover from unforeseen events rather than succeeding only in structured environments?
qs.n: Benchmark success overstates real autonomy: agents perform well on well-scoped tasks and fail on messy, underspecified ones. Recovery from novelty is what separates demos from deployable systems.

links.t: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Real World Tasks
AI Agents That Matter

qs.q: Will teams of agents compose into greater collective capability than any single system?
qs.n: Whether many agents compose into something greater is first a capability question: division of labor, communication protocols, emergent specialization. Early simulacra experiments show believable coordination; whether it scales into real collective intelligence is open. (The failure modes — collusion, correlated errors, cascades — are treated under Safety 2.4.)

links.t: Open Problems in Cooperative AI
Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior

qs.q: When will agents be able to earn and spend money, hire people, negotiate, operate businesses, and initiate further activity with little supervision?
qs.n: Agents already transact in sandboxes and small real deployments. The open questions are legal status, payment and identity infrastructure, and the point at which unsupervised economic initiative becomes routine.

links.t: Project Vend: Can Claude run a small shop?
Andreessen grants $50k to the semi-autonomous Truth Terminal project

qs.q: How readily can cognitive capability be converted into real-world power — money, influence, and control over infrastructure and institutions?
qs.n: The conversion crux beneath most takeover disagreements. One side maps concrete channels — earning money, hacking, recruiting human allies; the other holds that power is gated by deployment, permissions, trust, and institutions, so capability gains do not become power automatically. 1.3.5 tracks the economic milestone and 2.5.6 the catastrophic endpoint; this question owns the conversion mechanics both presuppose.

links.t: AI Could Defeat All of Us Combined
AI as Normal Technology
links.s: Narayanan & Kapoor, Knight First Amendment Institute

links.t: When should we worry about AI power-seeking?

qs.q: When will robots learn unfamiliar household, laboratory, industrial, or construction tasks from ordinary instructions?
qs.n: Vision-language-action models are the current bet that robotics follows the LLM playbook: broad foundation models plus fine-tuning, rather than task-specific engineering. Early results are promising and narrow.

links.t: π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model
Gemini Robotics: Bringing AI into the Physical World
Announcing Project GR00T, a “moonshot to solve embodied AGI” via a humanoid foundation model

qs.q: Can learning from video and simulation overcome the scarcity and expense of physical-world training data?
qs.n: Physical interaction data is scarce and costly to collect at internet scale. Whether video pretraining and simulation can substitute is the robotics analogue of the synthetic-data question — and similarly unresolved.

links.t: Sporks of AGI
Sim-to-Real Transfer in Deep RL for Robotics: a Survey

qs.q: Can robots become simultaneously capable, safe, inexpensive, and reliable in messy human environments?
qs.n: Skeptics argue touch-rich manipulation lacks both the data and the forgiving physics that made language tractable. Capable, safe, cheap, and reliable is a four-way tradeoff no one has yet closed in an open environment.

links.t: Why Today's Humanoids Won't Learn Dexterity
Robot Dexterity Still Seems Hard

qs.q: How capable will self-driving vehicles, drones, ships, and industrial machines become outside controlled settings?
qs.n: Driving is the furthest-deployed case of open-world embodied autonomy, with quantified safety records now public — a preview of the deployment, liability, and trust questions every other mobile system will face. (Military autonomy is treated under Safety 2.5 and Power 4.3.)

links.t: Waymo rider-only crash data vs. human benchmarks

qs.q: Will manipulation and unstructured environments keep embodied AI narrow, or will general physical competence eventually arrive?
qs.n: Skeptics argue touch-rich manipulation lacks both the data and the forgiving physics that made language tractable; market forecasts and engineering assessments currently point in different directions. (Labor-market consequences are treated under Economy 3.2.)

links.t: The global market for humanoid robots

qs.q: How much of model design, coding, experimentation, evaluation, and engineering can AI perform itself?
qs.n: AI R&D automation is simultaneously a capability frontier and a risk threshold in several frontier labs' safety frameworks. Current agents beat human experts on short research tasks and degrade on long ones.
qs.crux: Can AI substantially automate AI research and scientific discovery?

links.t: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities
AlphaEvolve: A coding agent for designing advanced algorithms
AI self-improvement will be a game-changer — and “extremely gradual across many years, probably a decade”

qs.q: Would AI-assisted AI research produce gradual acceleration or a discontinuous intelligence explosion?
qs.n: Takeoff debates increasingly hinge on a narrower question: whether software-only improvement can sustain acceleration while compute is fixed, or whether hardware cycles keep the feedback loop gradual.

links.t: Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead
A compute-centric framework for AI takeoff speeds
Will AI R&D Automation Cause a Software Intelligence Explosion?

qs.q: Can AI originate important hypotheses and conceptual frameworks rather than merely recombine existing knowledge?
qs.n: Blind-review studies find LLM-generated research ideas rated more novel than experts' — while skeptics argue paradigm-founding insight is different in kind from recombination. 'The Einstein question' remains open.

links.t: Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas?
The Einstein AI model

qs.q: Can agents autonomously generate hypotheses, run robotic experiments, analyze results, replicate findings, and choose subsequent experiments?
qs.n: Prototype systems have closed the loop in narrow chemistry and ML domains. Scaling to consequential science runs into verification, lab automation, and the cost of being wrong in the physical world.

links.t: Autonomous chemical research with LLMs (Coscientist)
The AI Scientist: Fully Automated Scientific Discovery

qs.q: What evidence would reveal that recursive acceleration or transformative scientific automation had begun?
qs.n: If recursion begins inside frontier labs, external indicators may lag badly. Scenario exercises try to specify what observable early signals — hiring, publication patterns, capability jumps — would look like.

links.t: Three Types of Intelligence Explosion
